key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the credit-card minimum-payment autopay option reduced minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, in part because it also reduced autopay enrollment and increased missed payments among liquidity-constrained cardholders.
methodology: Field experiment on credit card autopay enrollment with six-month follow-up.
why_it_matters: Shows that changing enrollment defaults for a liquid, self-directed consumer financial product can shift nominal enrollment behavior without changing the underlying financial outcome, and can even backfire via missed payments among liquidity-constrained users — directly bears on whether opt-out enrollment in round-up savings will produce real savings or just nominal sign-ups.
limitations: about credit card debt repayment, not savings accumulation
abstract gives no effect size on debt itself, only on payment behavior
relevance_reason: Directly tests a consumer financial nudge/default change with liquidity-constrained users and shows enrollment change decoupled from the real outcome — closest empirical analog to the round-up decision.

key_finding: Synthesizes the literature on defined-contribution plan design, including short- and long-term impacts of automatic enrollment and default investment options, and evidence of negative effects on participant engagement.
methodology: Narrative literature overview. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a recent synthesis of engagement costs from automatic enrollment defaults, useful context for weighing the disengagement risk our support team raises, though it stays within the employer-plan literature.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer app
overview rather than a primary study with effect sizes
relevance_reason: Recent review of default and auto-enrollment plan design effects and engagement costs, useful background even though not in our exact setting.

key_finding: Argues that while default enrollment raises short-term retirement plan participation, it also induces long-term passivity — low contribution rates, unmanaged accounts, and account churn — undermining welfare gains from participation alone.
methodology: Narrative policy discussion citing empirical literature. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly states the passivity/vanity-enrollment argument our support team is making, and proposes mitigations (auto-escalation, re-enrollment reminders) that could inform how we design an opt-out round-up default.
limitations: U.S. retirement system context, not consumer banking
no primary effect sizes given
relevance_reason: Explicitly frames default enrollment as a potential passive trap, directly supporting the counter-argument the brief asks us to test.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for downstream (later-in-time) effects of choice-architecture defaults on consumer behavior, identifying time course, prior preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators of whether default effects persist.
methodology: Conceptual/theoretical review synthesizing prior findings into a framework and research agenda. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a structured way to think about exactly the persistence/disengagement question the brief raises — which downstream outcomes to measure and what moderates whether a default's effect on enrollment translates into lasting engagement.
limitations: conceptual synthesis, not new empirical effect sizes
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: Directly addresses how and when default effects persist or fade over time in consumer settings, the core uncertainty the brief flags about vanity enrollment.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is remarkably insensitive even when the default option causes substantial losses.
methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options in a large administrative dataset.
why_it_matters: Provides credible causal evidence that default effects sustain over time and are insensitive to the default's quality — a caution against assuming users will actively correct a bad round-up default, though the mechanism (health insurance) differs from a financial app.
limitations: Medicare Part D drug plan setting, not consumer financial savings
low-income beneficiary population may differ from banking app users
relevance_reason: Strong causal evidence on persistence and insensitivity of default effects, a useful analog despite the different domain.

key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the measured effect of automatic enrollment and default contribution auto-escalation; steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from automatic enrollment and 0.3% from default auto-escalation, and only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first date.
methodology: Longitudinal analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job separation, balance withdrawal, and auto-escalation opt-out.
why_it_matters: The clearest statement of our support team's objection: the enrolment lift is real at signup and much smaller later — sets the ceiling our default-design decision should be measured against.
limitations: retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
abstract gives 401(k)-specific figures that may not map onto round-up savings
relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving amounts long-term, which the brief asked us to look for.

key_finding: Nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees in Germany's public pension raised participation by 23 percentage points, but most individuals subsequently actively opted out, with the default effect strongest for those with higher incentives or less awareness of their enrollment status.
methodology: Natural experiment using administrative and survey data around a nationwide auto-enrollment policy change.
why_it_matters: Shows a large headline enrollment lift is compatible with most people undoing the default once aware — cautions against reading a raw enrollment number as evidence the product works, echoing the support team's concern.
limitations: public pay-as-you-go pension system, not a consumer banking product
no data on amounts saved or persistence at 6-12 months of those who stayed
relevance_reason: Direct evidence that a large default-driven enrollment lift is undercut by active opt-out, informing how much weight to place on raw enrollment numbers.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's gains in retirement plan participation and contributions, replicated at 12 months, attenuate substantially by 36 months, with only modest average savings increases though a meaningful reduction in savings inequality.
methodology: Analysis of over 100 US retirement plans and a UK panel, plus a life-cycle consumption-savings model estimating switching costs (~$250).
why_it_matters: Directly quantifies how much a default's enrollment effect shrinks over a medium time horizon (36 months) versus 12 months, giving a concrete estimate of the persistence question that decides whether opt-out enrollment is worth building.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k) and UK pension plans, not a consumer savings app
structural model estimates depend on model assumptions
relevance_reason: Gives quantitative evidence on how much default enrollment effects fade by medium-term horizons, the central persistence question in the brief.

key_finding: In experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207), default options for risky-asset allocation produce medium-to-large effects on risk-taking, but implementing a default nudge (especially one the client would refuse) lowers the client's rating of the wealth manager's advice, with framing of the default question also shifting allocations.
methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative-sample experiment across five European countries testing default nudges and framing in investment decisions.
why_it_matters: Directly tests when a financial default reads as manipulative versus helpful in a European consumer-facing advisory context, showing defaults can damage trust — this is the exact dark-pattern/reputational risk the brief flags for our EU product, and cautions against a one-size-fits-all preset multiplier.
limitations: investment/wealth management context rather than a savings round-up feature
no follow-up beyond the initial decision, so persistence unmeasured
relevance_reason: European, consumer-facing financial-decision experiment directly measuring when a default is perceived as manipulative, exactly the reputational risk question the brief raises.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment raised 401(k) participation above 85% at three large firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default savings rate and conservative default fund, and half still did after three years, largely offsetting participation gains against low default-level anchoring.
methodology: Administrative panel data analysis across three large firms' 401(k) plans.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that people anchor heavily on a preset contribution level, not just on the enroll/don't-enroll default — the paper the anchoring-on-preset-levels literature still argues with, directly relevant to whether we should worry about the pre-set multiplier value.
limitations: employer 401(k) retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
predates smartphone/app-based products and current EU regulatory climate
relevance_reason: Foundational evidence that a preset contribution default anchors the level people end up at, directly relevant to the round-up multiplier decision, though from the classic employer-pension literature the brief says to treat with caution.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million taxi tipping decisions finds that 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost together (friction complementarity), and that adding an intermediate preset option (15% alongside 20-25-30%) captures 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at low revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on transaction data, validated with a stated-preference survey; counterfactual simulations of alternative default menus.
why_it_matters: Gives a rigorous account of why preset default menus anchor choices and how adding an intermediate preset option changes welfare — directly informs the question of which round-up multiplier to preset and whether adding more options helps or just adds friction.
limitations: tipping decisions on taxi rides, not a savings product
consumer self-directed but transactional context differs from an enrollment/savings decision
relevance_reason: A rigorous structural decomposition of why preset options anchor consumer choices, directly relevant to the round-up-multiplier preset decision, in a different consumer transactional setting.

key_finding: An opt-in short-term, liquid, withdraw-anytime payroll savings program at five UK firms saw very low take-up (at most 0.7% of eligible employees activated an account), but among those who did, 96% still had a positive balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at 12 months.
methodology: Field study of program introduction and administrative account data over the first 12 months, five UK firms.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the opt-in persistence question for a liquid short-term savings product, our closest real-world analog: opt-in take-up is very low, but retention among opt-ins is very high, suggesting opt-in enrollment may not be a vanity metric once someone actually signs up, though it also confirms the low-enrollment cost of pure opt-in.
limitations: payroll-deduction employer channel, so the employer-as-intermediary mechanism may partly drive take-up and cannot be fully separated from product design
does not report amounts saved beyond having a positive balance
relevance_reason: The closest empirical analog to the product being built — a liquid, withdraw-anytime, opt-in savings account — giving concrete opt-in take-up and 12-month retention figures.

key_finding: Provides a general theoretical characterization of optimal default options, showing that when the designer and choosers agree on an activity's value, a weighted form of opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, with extensions for externalities, fees, and normative ambiguity.
methodology: Theoretical model with asymptotic analysis and numerical simulations. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a normative framework for how to think about optimal default design, including when opt-out-minimizing versus other defaults are welfare-maximizing, relevant to justifying which entry design and preset level maximizes user welfare rather than just enrollment.
limitations: purely theoretical, no empirical application to a financial product
abstract does not specify population or setting
relevance_reason: General theory of optimal default design that could inform how to reason about welfare trade-offs in choosing entry and preset-level design, though not grounded in any specific consumer setting.

key_finding: Develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations to distinguish acceptable choice-architecture influence from regulable dark patterns under existing EU law.
methodology: Doctrinal legal analysis mapping EU statutes onto a normative autonomy framework; abstract-only, no empirical data.
why_it_matters: Gives the team a defensible EU legal test for whether an opt-out default (pre-selected enrollment or pre-selected multiplier) crosses from helpful default into a regulable dark pattern, directly informing how entry and level are framed and disclosed.
limitations: purely doctrinal/legal, no behavioral effect sizes
not specific to financial products or savings features
relevance_reason: Directly addresses the EU dark-pattern/manipulation risk the brief flags as a reputational constraint on the opt-out design.

key_finding: At a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had not opted out after 12 months (versus ~50% at lower defaults), and non-opters clustered at the suboptimal default rather than choosing higher matched contributions.
methodology: Administrative data analysis of a single employer retirement plan with a high default rate; includes a literature review of opt-out rates at lower defaults.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences that a pre-set level anchors people at a fixed point even when it is suboptimal for them, which is the exact risk the brief raises about defaulting the round-up multiplier.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a self-directed consumer product
the trusted-employer-intermediary mechanism the brief says does not carry over
relevance_reason: Strong anchoring evidence for decision 2, but capped for being an employer-plan setting rather than consumer self-directed.

key_finding: Title indicates four large UK field experiments on automating short-term payroll savings, but the abstract text provided is truncated/garbled and gives no extractable results.
methodology: abstract-only; abstract text is corrupted, so design and data are unknown beyond the title.
why_it_matters: If the full text matches the title, short-term (non-pension) automated savings experiments would be one of the closest analogues to a liquid round-up feature, but nothing can be verified from what is given.
limitations: abstract is not usable content, only a single word ('Trant')
cannot confirm effect sizes, population, or timeframe
relevance_reason: Topically close to the brief (short-term, liquid automated savings) but the record provides no usable evidence.

key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft alerts cuts unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, worth an estimated £170-240 million annually, though alerts still leave more than half of avoidable overdrafts unaddressed.
methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments run by major UK retail banks on live customer accounts.
why_it_matters: This is a consumer banking automatic-enrollment result, not a pension analogy: it shows defaults can move real financial behavior at scale in exactly our setting, while also showing a persistent gap between potential and realized benefit that supports the support team's disengagement concern.
limitations: measures charge avoidance, not savings amounts or a round-up product specifically
no explicit 6-12 month retention/withdrawal analysis
relevance_reason: The closest available consumer-banking automatic-enrollment evidence with real effect sizes, directly bearing on the entry decision.

key_finding: Over 41 months, each additional month of pension automatic enrollment raises average savings by £32-38 but also raises unsecured debt by £7 and mortgage balances by £118, partially offsetting the headline savings gain.
methodology: Randomized policy roll-out of automatic enrollment pensions across ~160,000 UK employers with 2-29 employees, tracked over 41 months.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the naive premise that default enrollment straightforwardly increases net financial wellbeing; shows a persistence/depth analysis is essential before treating enrollment as a win, which is exactly the support team's objection.
limitations: employer-mediated retirement pension, not a self-directed consumer app
debt offset mechanism may not transfer to a liquid, easily-withdrawn round-up pot
relevance_reason: Best available longitudinal evidence that default-driven saving has offsetting costs, informing the C5/C2 questions, capped for the employer-pension setting.

key_finding: Adding a minor enrollment 'ordeal' to health insurance auto-enrollment cut enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people, and a selection model shows such ordeals do not efficiently screen out low-value enrollees.
methodology: Natural experiment studying removal of an auto-enrollment health insurance policy, with a theoretical selection-market model.
why_it_matters: Warns that adding friction (akin to opt-in or active choice) to remove a default can disproportionately exclude exactly the people the feature is meant to help, a distributional risk relevant to weighing opt-in against opt-out or active choice.
limitations: health insurance selection market, not consumer banking
adverse-selection framing may not apply to a savings feature with no insurer counterpart
relevance_reason: Strong analogy on the harms of removing defaults/adding friction and on distributional impact, capped for being outside the financial-consumer setting.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults on political campaign websites raised donations by over $43 million but also increased refund requests by almost $3 million, with the largest effects on smaller, less-experienced donors who did not compensate by changing donation amounts.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design across multiple 2020 US campaign websites that added pre-checked recurring-donation boxes at different times.
why_it_matters: A near-perfect consumer-digital analogue to a pre-checked enrollment default: it shows a default can raise nominal sign-ups while generating complaints/refunds and disproportionately affecting inexperienced users, mirroring the support team's exact worry about the round-up feature.
limitations: political donations rather than personal savings
refund/complaint outcome is a proxy for disengagement, not a direct engagement or withdrawal measure
relevance_reason: Directly tests default effects on amount and heterogeneity in a self-directed consumer digital-payment setting close to the brief's own concerns.

key_finding: A default option raises the reservation utility that triggers active search, and those who search past the default indeed find higher-ranked options, supporting both a reference-dependence effect and a self-selection effect.
methodology: Laboratory choice experiment testing a reference-dependent search model against a control condition without self-selection.
why_it_matters: Offers a mechanism for why people who reject a default (as in active choice) tend to end up with better-suited choices, relevant to whether active choice captures benefits without the passive-enrollment downside.
limitations: generic abstract lab task, no specified financial or consumer-app context
no measure of enrollment, persistence, or amount saved
relevance_reason: Provides a theoretical mechanism for the active-choice question, capped for being an unrelated abstract laboratory setting.

key_finding: Mandated browser choice screens under the EU Digital Markets Act raised Firefox usage 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects persisting from 15 months after rollout onward.
methodology: Difference-in-differences analysis around the staggered EU DMA choice-screen mandate across iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: Real-world evidence that a regulator-mandated active choice screen produces large, persistent behavior change in a mobile app setting under EU law — the closest available test of whether active choice meaningfully counters entrenched defaults in exactly our regulatory and device context.
limitations: browser selection, not a financial savings decision
no measure of user-reported satisfaction, complaints, or disengagement
relevance_reason: Directly evidences the persistence and magnitude of active-choice effects in a mobile app, EU-regulated context, bearing on decision 1.

key_finding: A usability study of nine active-choice (non-default) opt-out interface designs found generalizable schemes reduce disruption substantially (98% of participants felt undisrupted with the best scheme, a 40-point improvement) at only a slight cost to opt-out utility.
methodology: Browser-extension usability study with 410 participants comparing nine active-choice privacy interface designs, no defaults permitted by law.
why_it_matters: Offers concrete interface-design lessons for building a low-friction, non-manipulative active-choice screen if the team avoids defaults entirely for legal or reputational reasons.
limitations: privacy opt-out under CCPA/GPC, not a financial enrollment decision
no measure of downstream financial engagement or amounts
relevance_reason: Relevant design guidance for building active choice well, capped for being a privacy-law rather than financial-product setting.

key_finding: Switching university exam sign-up to opt-out raised sign-ups but had no effect on effortful outcomes (exam preparation, passing) for most students, with gains concentrated among students who were already responsive to university communication.
methodology: Two field experiments changing exam sign-up to opt-out in two study programs, comparing treated and control students' downstream effort and pass rates.
why_it_matters: Directly supports the support team's worry: a default can lift nominal sign-up numbers while doing nothing for the people who need to actually engage, and may even be vanity metric-generating for non-responsive individuals.
limitations: university exam administration, not a financial product
effortful task differs from a savings-contribution decision in structure
relevance_reason: Best available evidence that opt-out enrollment gains do not translate into effortful downstream engagement for everyone, directly bearing on the enrollment-vs-engagement trade-off, capped for setting.

key_finding: After target-date funds became a default retirement investment option post-PPA, younger and older workers' stock allocations shifted to track the TDF glidepath, but contribution rates changed little.
methodology: Account-level panel data on millions of US middle-class investors, 2006-2018, exploiting the Pension Protection Act's default-option rule change.
why_it_matters: Shows a preset default can anchor the composition/level of a financial choice (asset allocation) even while leaving the underlying contribution amount unmoved, a useful caution that a preset multiplier might reshape behavior without changing overall saved amounts.
limitations: employer retirement plan investment defaults, not a consumer savings multiplier
outcome is portfolio allocation, not enrollment or withdrawal behavior
relevance_reason: Analogous evidence on default anchoring of a chosen level, capped for the employer-retirement setting.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT on voluntary pension saving in China, all tested nudges including default options significantly reduced willingness to contribute relative to control, contrary to prevailing international evidence, with the largest backfire from positive-narrative and default nudges.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, default, and narrative nudges on voluntary pension contribution decisions.
why_it_matters: A direct empirical contradiction of the 'defaults always help' premise the brief asks us to test, in a self-directed voluntary-savings decision context with reported heterogeneity by income, education, and gender.
limitations: voluntary pension saving in China, cultural/institutional context may differ from EU consumer banking
online survey stated intentions rather than live product enrollment or actual money
relevance_reason: Directly requested by the brief: a study contradicting the assumption that defaults reliably raise saving, with distributional detail on who is helped or hurt.

key_finding: In a pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians, people rate financial nudges positively overall, prefer System 2 (deliberative) interventions and savings-framed messaging over spending-framed messaging, and transparency has no significant effect on approval.
methodology: Pre-registered survey experiment with 36 hypothetical scenarios varying transparency, framing, and System 1/2 targeting; six dependent variables including approval and perceived manipulation.
why_it_matters: Directly informs how to frame and communicate the round-up enrolment choice (savings framing preferred, System 2/deliberate framing preferred) to avoid a dark-pattern reputational risk, and shows disclosure of mechanism need not hurt approval.
limitations: hypothetical vignettes, not actual product behaviour
Australian sample, not EU
does not measure enrolment or persistence outcomes
relevance_reason: Speaks directly to whether a default or nudge reads as helpful vs manipulative, the EU reputational-risk question the brief raises.

key_finding: Offering CCT beneficiaries the choice of bank-account delivery had no significant average effect on savings, but raised balances specifically among those with nonpositive prior balances.
methodology: Field experiment on conditional cash transfer beneficiaries randomised to cash vs. bank-account delivery, abstract-only detail.
why_it_matters: Suggests defaults/choice architecture around account-based saving may only move people who were previously non-savers, relevant to who benefits from a round-up default, but the population and context are far from a consumer banking app.
limitations: conditional cash transfer recipients in a developing-economy context, not consumer banking app users
no measure of default vs opt-in enrolment mechanism
abstract gives no effect sizes for headline result
relevance_reason: Touches on distributional heterogeneity in who savings interventions help, echoing the brief's concern about who is helped vs hurt.

key_finding: Compares contribution cases with identical amounts but differing liquid-fund withdrawal rules under a universal automatic IRA with an emergency savings component.
methodology: abstract-only; appears to be an administrative/policy comparison of automatic IRA program variants.
why_it_matters: Touches the liquidity question (locking vs. keeping funds withdrawable) that is central to whether a round-up pot behaves like a savings account or a locked pension, but the abstract fragment gives too little detail to use directly.
limitations: abstract is a fragment lacking key results
automatic IRA is a policy-level, quasi-employer intervention, not a self-directed app
no information on enrolment method effect size
relevance_reason: Nominally relevant to liquid emergency savings design but abstract too thin to extract usable evidence.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrolment dramatically raised participation, and most auto-enrolled participants stuck to the default contribution rate and default fund allocation even years later, often treating the default as implicit advice.
methodology: Natural experiment comparing 401(k) savings behaviour before and after a single large US firm switched from opt-in to automatic enrolment; administrative data.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that defaults both raise enrolment and anchor the contribution level people end up at — directly the anchoring risk the brief asks about for the round-up multiplier — but the employer-as-advisor mechanism does not transfer to a self-directed app.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app
the 'default as investment advice' mechanism relies on employer trust that the brief says does not carry over
20+ years old, predates current fintech and EU regulatory context
relevance_reason: The classic anchoring/default-persistence result the literature on this topic argues with; scored against but not for our exact setting.

key_finding: Compares savings behaviours between automatically enrolled and voluntarily enrolled participants in defined-contribution retirement plans (no abstract available to state effect sizes).
methodology: abstract-only; presumably an observational comparison of DC plan participants under different enrolment regimes.
why_it_matters: Potentially another data point on auto vs. voluntary enrolment savings behaviour, but with no abstract there is nothing concrete to weigh against our decision.
limitations: no abstract text available, so no verifiable findings
employer-sponsored DC retirement plan, not a consumer app
forthcoming 2026 publication, unclear final content
relevance_reason: Title matches the enrolment-mechanism question but content cannot be assessed from the record provided.

key_finding: Low institutional trust and minority/non-national status are both associated with under-saving and with early withdrawal of retirement savings once a withdrawal option becomes available, a 'double jeopardy' for the same vulnerable group.
methodology: Analysis of three representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) around a pension reform introducing early withdrawal, linking trust and nationality to both saving and withdrawal decisions.
why_it_matters: Directly relevant to the support team's worry about passively-enrolled users withdrawing money quickly and to the brief's demand for distributional analysis of who is helped vs. hurt by a default, since it shows the same low-trust group both under-saves and withdraws early.
limitations: mandatory pension scheme reform, not a consumer opt-in/opt-out fintech product
withdrawal driven by a policy reform, not by product design choices
Estonian pension context, not EU consumer banking app
relevance_reason: Provides direct evidence on the withdrawal/disengagement and distributional-harm questions the brief poses, even though the setting is a mandatory pension scheme rather than our app.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent G7 survey experiment, prompting people to reflect on being automatically enrolled in a default policy reduced their stated intentions to comply and reduced approval of the policy, contrary to the assumption that defaults simply and quietly help.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment across G7 countries testing reflection prompts about a hypothetical default-enrolment vaccination booster policy.
why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the internal 'defaults always help' assumption: making people aware of, or reflect on, an automatic-enrolment design can trigger backlash and lower approval, a live risk for an opt-out round-up rollout in an EU consumer-protection climate.
limitations: public-health vaccination policy setting, not a financial product
hypothetical policy vignette rather than actual enrolment behaviour
no measure of enrolment or savings amount effects
relevance_reason: Explicitly contradicts the premise that awareness of a default is harmless, which the brief asked us to test against.

key_finding: Among US Millennials, automatic enrolment and employer contribution provisions are associated with a higher likelihood of retirement plan participation, while their absence is linked to non-participation.
methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of the 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study controlling for debt, income, risk tolerance and assets.
why_it_matters: Adds another confirmatory data point that auto-enrolment raises participation, but offers nothing new on persistence, anchoring, or active choice that would change our design.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan context
cross-sectional/correlational, not a natural or randomized experiment
no data on amount saved, withdrawal, or active-choice comparison
relevance_reason: Confirms the well-established default enrolment effect but adds little decision-relevant information for a consumer app.

key_finding: Using 41 million observations in Denmark, automatic (passive) employer contributions raised savings substantially, while tax subsidies requiring active choice mostly just shifted assets between accounts (each $1 of subsidy raised total saving by only 1 cent); ~85% of people are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but moved by automatic defaults, and active savers are wealthier and more sophisticated.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data analysis of Danish retirement savings accounts distinguishing active vs. passive responses to subsidies and automatic contributions.
why_it_matters: Provides the clearest quantitative evidence that passive/default mechanisms move money much more than active-choice-requiring incentives, and that the people who need help most (unsophisticated, less wealthy) are the ones defaults reach — a key input into whether opt-out or active choice is the right call, and to whom it matters.
limitations: Danish tax-advantaged retirement accounts, not a liquid consumer savings product
shifts are about which account money sits in more than app-level enrolment/opt-in design
predates the fintech/EU regulatory context the brief specifies
relevance_reason: The key evidentiary basis for the active-vs-passive distinction underlying the opt-in/opt-out/active-choice decision, and for who is helped vs. hurt by defaults, despite being in a pension-account setting.

key_finding: Proposes and field-tests 'enhanced active choice' — a forced-choice design that highlights the losses of the non-preferred option — as an alternative to automatic enrolment that can nudge behaviour without a default.
methodology: Review of prior active-choice literature plus two original field experiments testing standard active choice vs. enhanced (loss-framed) active choice against no intervention.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, testable design for the active-choice arm of the entry decision: forcing a yes/no answer while loss-framing the 'no round-up' option could capture much of the opt-out enrolment benefit without the disengagement risk of true auto-enrolment.
limitations: field experiments are in medication adherence, not financial savings
does not report enrolment persistence or amount saved at 6-12 months
no direct test in a consumer banking or fintech context
relevance_reason: The specific mechanism transfers directly to the entry-design decision: 'enhanced active choice' is a concrete alternative to opt-out that the brief's active-choice question is asking about.

key_finding: Synthesizes the behavioural household finance literature across savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance, and reviews interventions including choice architecture, product design, and disclosure that firms and governments use to shape financial behaviour.
methodology: Narrative literature review/book chapter (NBER), abstract-only detail on specific effect sizes.
why_it_matters: Gives the broad map of which choice-architecture levers (defaults, product design, disclosure) have evidence behind them in consumer finance generally, useful for sanity-checking that our two design decisions are the right ones to focus scarce evidence-gathering on.
limitations: broad narrative review without a systematic protocol
abstract does not give effect sizes specific to round-up savings or active choice
covers household finance broadly rather than fintech-app enrolment specifically
relevance_reason: The review/synthesis anchor giving a landscape of behavioural household-finance interventions, the kind of overview the brief asks for alongside single-study evidence.

key_finding: Automatic enrolment pushed 401(k) participation above 85% at three firms, but roughly 80% of participants initially accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and default conservative fund, with half still at the default after three years, largely offsetting participation gains against low default-level savings.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large US firms comparing automatic vs. voluntary 401(k) enrolment.
why_it_matters: The clearest classic evidence that a pre-set default level anchors most people for years, which is the direct precedent for worrying that a pre-selected round-up multiplier will anchor users at whatever level we pick rather than at their true preference.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k), not a consumer app
over two decades old, predates current fintech/regulatory context
locked retirement savings rather than liquid, withdrawable funds
relevance_reason: Foundational evidence for the anchoring risk on the preset-multiplier decision, the paper this literature line still argues with.

key_finding: Randomly assigning employees to different default savings-account enrolment options increased participation by 40 percentage points, an effect equivalent to a 50% matching incentive, driven mainly by present bias and the cognitive cost of thinking through savings scenarios, and defaults also increased subsequent active/voluntary saving.
methodology: Field experiment randomising default enrolment variants of a salary-linked savings account among employees in Afghanistan, with follow-up interventions to isolate mechanisms.
why_it_matters: Gives a rare mechanistic account of *why* defaults work (present bias, cognitive cost) rather than just that they work, useful for judging whether defaults in our app would be genuinely helpful (overcoming inertia) or just nominal, and shows defaults can increase later active engagement rather than only crowding it out.
limitations: salary-linked accounts in an employer/development context, not a fully self-directed consumer app
developing-economy setting far from an EU regulatory and liquidity context
no measure of long-run withdrawal or complaint behaviour
relevance_reason: Provides an unusually direct test of default mechanisms (present bias, cognitive cost) relevant to judging whether an opt-out design would help or just inflate enrolment numbers.

key_finding: A field experiment with a financial-management platform found payment reminders cut late-payment fees by 14% overall but raised overdraft fees by 9%, concentrated in users with an overdraft history, who saw a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment on a consumer financial-management platform in Brazil comparing reminder vs. no-reminder groups, tracking downstream fee outcomes across products.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the support team's concern that a well-intentioned nudge can help most users on average while actively harming a vulnerable subgroup — exactly the heterogeneity risk the brief says we must check before defaulting everyone into round-up savings.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrollment defaults or preset contribution levels
credit card/overdraft context rather than round-up savings
no long-horizon (6-12 month) persistence data reported in abstract
relevance_reason: Best available evidence in a consumer financial self-directed setting for the brief's explicit worry about who is helped versus hurt by nudge-style interventions.
